case_studies.title: Contagion Networks: Evaluator Bias Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
case_studies.abstract: When large language models serve as evaluators in multi-agent systems, their systematic evaluation biases propagate through the agent network. We introduce Contagion Networks, a formal framework for measuring how evaluator biases spread across interacting LLM agents. In a controlled 3-agent experiment using DeepSeek-chat with three distinct evaluator bias profiles (structured, balanced, evidence-based), we measure the Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Gamma_3 and find that evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents (gamma in [0.157, 0.352]), even within the same underlying model. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluator bias in large language models, introducing Contagion Networks to measure how biases spread between agents. It builds a framework to assess bias propagation in multi-agent systems. The result shows that evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents, even within the same model.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on natural language processing and large language models, but IT managers working with AI and machine learning systems may want to consider the implications of evaluator bias on their models.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper discusses LLM evaluator bias propagation, relevant to IT deployment of AI systems. Could be used to flag potential security risks or improve AI performance. Relies on DeepSeek-chat, which may not be widely used. Could be applied to a range of multi-agent systems.

case_studies.title: Multi-LCB: Extending LiveCodeBench to Multiple Programming Languages
case_studies.abstract: LiveCodeBench (LCB) has recently become a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on code-generation tasks. By curating competitive programming problems, constantly adding fresh problems to the set, and filtering them by release dates, LCB provides contamination-aware evaluation and offers a holistic view of coding capability. However, LCB remains restricted to Python, leaving open the question of whether LLMs can generalize across the diverse programming languages required in real-world software engineering. We introduce Multi-LCB, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of limited programming language support in LiveCodeBench, a benchmark for evaluating large language models. The authors built Multi-LCB, which extends LiveCodeBench to support multiple programming languages. The result is a more comprehensive evaluation of language models' code-generation capabilities.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on evaluating large language models for code-generation tasks, rather than addressing specific cloud infrastructure management needs.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces Multi-LCB, which is relevant to IT engineers working with LLMs, and has the potential for use in software engineering, making it valuable within 90 days. However, novelty is not extremely high due to the extension of an existing benchmark, rather than entirely new research.

case_studies.title: Human-on-the-Loop Orchestration for AI-Assisted Legal Discovery
case_studies.abstract: Autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in electronic discovery (e-discovery), where compounding errors across multi-step reasoning chains can constitute legal malpractice. Unlike single-turn retrieval, agentic workflows operating over privileged document corpora exhibit a class of failure we term "trajectory collapse": an early misclassification silently propagates, rendering an entire privilege review invalid. case_studies.title: Formal Verification of Learned Multi-Agent Communication Policies via Decision Tree Distillation
case_studies.abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables agents to develop coordination strategies through emergent communication, but neural policies lack the formal safety guarantees required for safety-critical robotic deployment in drone swarms and autonomous vehicle fleets. We present the first end-to-end framework for safety verification of learned multi-agent communication policies through policy abstraction: neural policies are distilled into interpretable decision trees, then formally verified, with empirical validation confirming that verified safety properties transfer to original networks
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of ensuring safety in multi-agent systems like drone swarms and autonomous vehicle fleets by verifying the communication policies between agents. The researchers built a framework that converts complex neural network policies into simpler decision trees, which can be formally verified for safety. The result is a more reliable way to ensure safety-critical systems work correctly.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on robotic deployment and autonomous vehicle fleets, but IT professionals working with clients in these industries may find it relevant to discuss potential applications and benefits.
case_studies.score_reasoning: While not directly relevant to IT infrastructure tools, this paper reveals novel insights into safety guarantees required for AI systems. IT engineers might find it useful in understanding requirements for deploying AI in safety-critical systems, but it's unlikely to affect their day-to-day work. case_studies.title: UltraQuant: 4-bit KV Caching for Context-Heavy Agents
case_studies.abstract: Context-heavy agents place unusual pressure on the key-value (KV) cache: long prefixes are reused across many short turns, while concurrency determines whether the serving system can keep GPUs utilized. We study 4-bit KV-cache compression for this setting, using TurboQuant-style rotation and codebook quantization as a quality anchor and vLLM FP8 KV caching as the deployment anchor. We report three contributions. First, we frame 4-bit KV caching around multi-round agent workloads where task quality, cache residency, and serving throughput must be measured jointly. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of key-value cache compression for context-heavy agents, building a 4-bit KV caching system called UltraQuant, which results in improved cache residency and serving throughput. The system uses TurboQuant-style rotation and codebook quantization to compress the cache. This research is relevant to IT engineers managing cloud infrastructure that supports artificial intelligence or machine learning workloads.

case_studies.title: AgentFinVQA: A Deployable Multi-Agent Pipeline for Auditable Financial Chart QA
case_studies.abstract: Financial chart question answering in regulated settings demands more than accuracy: practitioners must know which answers to trust before acting on them, and many institutions cannot send client data to external model providers. Yet existing chart-QA agents are accuracy-focused and opaque, and most assume proprietary API access; to our knowledge, none combines auditability with on-premise deployability without significant accuracy compromise. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of trustworthy financial chart question answering in regulated settings by building AgentFinVQA, a multi-agent pipeline that provides auditable and deployable results. The pipeline achieves this without compromising accuracy and can be deployed on-premise. This result allows financial institutions to verify answers before acting on them.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage financial data systems, here is what to consider: check if your current chart-QA solutions provide auditable and transparent results, assess if AgentFinVQA can be integrated into your on-premise infrastructure, and evaluate its potential to improve trust in financial chart question answering.
